content: To build a clean government, you must start with three things: first, be utterly incorruptible yourself; second, pay ministers and civil servants high market wages so they are not tempted; third, make the penalty for corruption severe and ensure certainty of punishment.

A small nation cannot afford the luxury of being emotional in foreign policy. Singapore must be a 'poison shrimp'—indispensable, useful to major powers, and resilient enough that swallowing us causes more trouble than it is worth.
I have always tried to be correct, not politically correct. A leader must look at the world as it is, not as we wish it to be. Pragmatism is about finding what works, regardless of ideology.

Meritocracy ensures that the best minds rise to the top regardless of their parents' wealth or status. Without education and human capital, Singapore has nothing; our people are our only natural resource.

When Singapore was abruptly expelled from Malaysia in 1965, we were suddenly independent without a natural resource or even an adequate water supply. Survival was not guaranteed. We had to create a rugged society, build an economy from scratch, and convince the world that a tiny, multiracial island could be a viable, sovereign state.

In a multiracial society like Singapore, you cannot afford to let language, race, or religion become fault lines. We instituted strict bilingualism and housing quotas to ensure that every community lives side by side, forcing integration rather than allowing communal enclaves to divide us.

content: Small nations must be exceptionally clear-eyed about major powers. Do not take sides blindly. We maintain friendly ties with both the United States and China, because neutrality and open trade are the lifeblood of our economy.

Life is not a game of fair outcomes; it is about striving against the odds. There is no substitute for discipline, rigorous preparation, and relentless hard work. Good luck is often just preparation meeting opportunity.
